name: Azelaic acid scalp
lead: Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid used topically at 15 to 20 percent for acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation.[1] In hair-loss communities it is applied to the scalp or included in compounded anti-hair-loss lotions with the aim of slowing thinning and keeping hair density, because of claims that it mildly inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme targeted by finasteride and dutasteride.[3][4]

Wikipedia cites a 1988 in vitro report in which azelaic acid combined with zinc sulfate strongly inhibited 5-alpha-reductase in human skin; the article notes this is a single in vitro study and not clinical evidence that topical azelaic acid alone has this effect in vivo.[1] A forum poster in 2000 asked about a French study combining zinc, vitamin B6 and azelaic acid reported to lower scalp DHT, showing how the idea circulated early.[5]

A small early phase 1 trial of azelaic acid in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a scarring alopecia, is registered.[2] Lifting forums mention azelaic acid in compounded topical mixes with minoxidil, tretinoin and finasteride, usually discussed by people also dealing with hair thinning from anabolic use.[3][6]
infobox: Wheat, rye, barley; produced by Malassezia furfur[1]

paras: Topical azelaic acid is used for mild to moderate acne, both comedonal and inflammatory, and for papulopustular rosacea. It is also used for melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, particularly in people with darker skin types, and has been recommended as an alternative to hydroquinone [1]. Wikipedia cites a 1996 review claiming 20 percent azelaic acid matched 4 percent hydroquinone over three months and that combination with tretinoin did better still [1]. Preparations and research typically use 15 to 20 percent, and in moderate acne twice-daily 20 percent cream for three months significantly reduced comedones, papules and pustules, with results typically appearing after about four weeks [1].

Because it lowers acne lesions and inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme in melanin synthesis, azelaic acid is used to even out skin tone and reduce blemishes on the face [1]. In hair communities, people apply it to the scalp or include it in compounded anti-hair-loss lotions aiming to slow thinning and keep hair density [3][4]. No approved hair-loss indication exists for azelaic acid, so scalp use is off-label.

Azelaic acid is bacteriostatic against Cutibacterium acnes and Staphylococcus epidermidis by disrupting microbial metabolism and membrane pH balance, and the account in Wikipedia notes this does not promote bacterial resistance. In keratinocytes it inhibits DNA, RNA and protein synthesis, normalising follicular keratinisation and helping prevent comedones, and it lowers reactive oxygen species and pro-inflammatory cytokines [1].

The hair-loss rationale rests on a 1988 in vitro study in which azelaic acid combined with zinc sulfate inhibited 5-alpha-reductase by about 90 percent, a level comparable to finasteride and dutasteride in that assay [1]. 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the androgen implicated in pattern hair loss. Wikipedia presents this only as laboratory evidence. Separate mid-1980s laboratory research found depigmenting effects only at high concentrations that were cytotoxic to melanocytes [1].

Azelaic acid (nonanedioic acid, C9H16O4) is a saturated dicarboxylic acid and a white powder. It occurs naturally in wheat, rye and barley and is produced by the skin yeast Malassezia furfur. Industrially it is made by ozonolysis of oleic acid and is used in polymers such as nylon-6,9, plasticizers and lubricant thickeners as well as some hair and skin conditioners [1].
Skin dryness and irritation are the main reported effects of topical use, particularly in people with eczema [1]. Its hazard classification carries warnings for skin and serious eye irritation [1].

Brands listed include Azelex, Finacea, Skinoren, Finevin, Azelan and Azaclear (combined with niacinamide) [1]. It is prescription-only in the United States and listed as Schedule 5 in Australia [1]. It ranked 309th among prescribed medicines in the United States in 2023, with more than 200,000 prescriptions [1].

subs.h: Use in hair-loss and lifting communities
paras: On T Nation, azelaic acid comes up in threads about hair loss during testosterone therapy or anabolic cycles, where members list options beyond the 'big 3' of finasteride, minoxidil and ketoconazole shampoo [6][7]. One poster suggests having a compounding pharmacy mix 10 percent minoxidil, tretinoin, azelaic acid, 0.1 percent finasteride, biotin and hydrocortisone into a single lotion, and another asks whether topical azelaic acid cream can control scalp DHT for someone on testosterone therapy [3][4]. A 2000 post asked about a French study said to have lowered scalp DHT by 90 percent with zinc, vitamin B6 and azelaic acid [5]. These are personal and secondhand accounts.

A registered early phase 1 trial (NCT05416333) is testing azelaic acid in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a scarring alopecia, in 18 participants. It began on 12 August 2024 and is listed as active, not recruiting; no results have been posted [2]. No studies found of azelaic acid for androgenetic alopecia. For skin, azelaic acid has trials in acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation, summarised in the medical-use section [1].

timeline.event: In vitro report of azelaic acid plus zinc sulfate inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase.[1]

lore.intro: Azelaic acid appears in T Nation hair-loss threads and compounded-topical suggestions as a mild 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid on the scalp acts as a mild 5-ARI and lowers scalp DHT.
claims.believers: Posters cite a French study said to lower scalp DHT with zinc, B6 and azelaic acid and say they have heard it can control scalp DHT.[4][5]
claims.experts: The cited inhibition was an in vitro finding with zinc sulfate; no clinical evidence of this effect from topical use alone is described.[1]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid can be combined with minoxidil, tretinoin and finasteride in a compounded lotion.
claims.believers: One T Nation member recommends a compounding pharmacy mix that includes azelaic acid alongside other actives.[3]
claims.experts: No published trial of such a mixture including azelaic acid for pattern hair loss was found; its registered scalp trial concerns CCCA.[2]

card.summary: Acne/rosacea acid with a lab-only 5-ARI claim, used in hair stacks without scalp trials for pattern hair loss.

quick.overview:
Azelaic acid is a skin treatment for acne and rosacea. Some hair-loss users put it on the scalp for a claimed mild finasteride-like effect.

The claim comes from a 1988 lab study; no pattern-hair-loss trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It reduces bacteria, inflammation and pigment production; 5-alpha-reductase inhibition was shown in vitro in combination with zinc sulfate.
quick.risks: Dryness and irritation are the main reported effects.

chain: Applied to scalp, often within a compounded topical
Proposed mild local 5-alpha-reductase inhibition, lowering scalp DHT
Slower thinning and better hair density, claimed rather than shown
angle.text: Hair-loss forum members add azelaic acid to scalp stacks hoping for a mild anti-DHT effect that helps preserve hair. The supporting data cited are a 1988 laboratory result; scalp trials in pattern hair loss have not been published.
